title: Cloud Migration Planning: A Practical Selection and Implementation Guide
description: A step-by-step cloud migration planning guide for inventory, dependencies, security, data transfer, cutover, rollback, cost control, and post-migration validation.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Build an accurate inventory
sections.body: List applications, databases, file stores, scheduled jobs, identities, network dependencies, external APIs, certificates, and operational owners. For each workload, record business criticality, data sensitivity, peak demand, recovery objectives, support status, and maintenance windows. Discover dependencies from configuration and runtime telemetry where possible instead of relying only on interviews. An incomplete inventory is a common reason migrations miss hidden batch jobs, integrations, or licensing constraints.

sections.title: Choose a migration approach per workload
sections.body: Classify each workload according to whether it should be rehosted, replatformed, refactored, replaced, retained temporarily, or retired. Rehosting can reduce initial change but may preserve inefficiencies; refactoring can improve long-term fit but usually increases scope and testing effort. Record the reason, expected benefit, cost, risks, and rollback options for each decision. Avoid forcing every application into the same pattern simply to make the plan look consistent.

sections.title: Design identity, network, and security
sections.body: Define account or subscription boundaries, network connectivity, DNS, identity federation, privileged access, secret management, encryption, logging, backup, and incident response before moving production data. Identify any public endpoints and make their access requirements explicit. Test least-privilege roles and service identities in the target environment. Map data residency, retention, and regulatory requirements to the actual services and regions being selected.

sections.title: Plan data movement and integrity checks
sections.body: Measure data volume, change rate, transfer bandwidth, downtime tolerance, and the consistency guarantees of the source and destination. Decide whether data will move in one transfer, incremental batches, replication, or a maintenance-window cutover. Validate record counts, checksums where appropriate, schema compatibility, permissions, and application-level invariants. Preserve a known-good source copy until reconciliation is complete and the business owner accepts the migrated data.

sections.title: Rehearse cutover and rollback
sections.body: Write a runbook with named owners, time estimates, communication steps, decision points, and exact validation commands. Rehearse the procedure in a staging environment using production-like volumes. Define a go/no-go checkpoint and rollback triggers such as failed integrity checks, unacceptable latency, or broken critical transactions. Rollback must account for writes made after cutover; switching DNS back does not automatically reconcile divergent data.

sections.title: Control cost and validate operations
sections.body: Estimate compute, storage, network egress, managed services, backup, observability, support, and licensing under normal and peak load. Configure budgets, alerts, resource tags, and ownership before workloads arrive. After cutover, validate user journeys, performance, access controls, backups, restore tests, monitoring, and support escalation. Compare actual cost and reliability with the baseline after the first billing cycle, then close the migration only when the operational owner accepts the service.
